title: Enumerations Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing enumerations, which make arbitrary integer codes more readable in C++ programs.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the topic of Enumerations. The subtitle states: Make arbitrary integer codes more readable. Enumerations provide a way to associate meaningful symbolic names with integer values, improving code clarity and maintainability.
notes_text: Enumerations are introduced before structs because they are often used as data members within structs. For example, a student struct might use an enumeration for the major field rather than raw integer codes.

title: Enumerations Syntax and Usage
summary: Enumerations associate integers with symbolic names using the enum keyword. The compiler assigns sequential values starting from 0.
main_text: An enumeration associates an integer (number) with a symbolic name. The syntax is: enum [optional_collection_name] {Item1, Item2, ... ItemN}. Item1 = 0, Item2 = 1, and so on up to ItemN = N-1. You use symbolic item names in your code and the compiler will replace the symbolic names with corresponding integer values. Without enumerations, you would need to hard code symbolic names with const int declarations like: const int BLACK=0; const int BROWN=1; const int RED=2; const int WHITE=7; With enumerations, you simplify this to: enum Colors {BLACK, BROWN, RED, ..., WHITE}; Then int pixela = RED; assigns pixela the value 2, and int pixelb = BROWN; assigns pixelb the value 1. Another example: enum {CSCI, CSBA, CECS, CSGM, BUAI, QBIO}; allows int major = BUAI; which sets major to 4, and int minor = CSCI; which sets minor to 0. Use enumerations to make related integer codes and constants more readable.
notes_text: Enumerations are especially useful when you have a fixed set of related constants. The compiler automatically assigns sequential integer values starting from 0 unless you explicitly specify values. You can also assign custom starting values. Enumerations improve code maintenance because adding a new item automatically adjusts all subsequent values.

images.description: Code examples showing three approaches: hard-coded const int declarations, using enum to simplify color definitions, and using enum for university majors. Each demonstrates how enumerations replace manual integer assignments.
labels: enum {CSCI, CSBA, CECS, CSGM, BUAI, QBIO}

title: Objects Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the concept of objects in C++ programming.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the topic of Objects. Objects are a fundamental concept in C++ that will be explored in detail throughout Unit 3.
notes_text: This section transitions from enumerations to the core topic of the unit: understanding what objects are, why they are useful, and how they are implemented in C++ using structs and later classes.

title: Review: Program Decomposition - Procedural vs Object-Oriented
summary: C uses procedural decomposition with functions, while C++ adds object-oriented constructs where classes/objects are the primary unit of organization.
main_text: C is a procedural language where a function or procedure is the primary unit of code organization, problem decomposition, and abstraction. Functions can be reused across many applications. C++ is considered an object-oriented language that adds object-oriented constructs to C, though it still supports a procedural approach. In C++, a class or object is the primary unit of code organization, problem decomposition, and abstraction. Classes and objects can also be reused across applications.
notes_text: Understanding the difference between procedural and object-oriented approaches is crucial. In procedural programming, you think about what actions (verbs) need to be performed. In object-oriented programming, you think about what entities (nouns) exist in your problem domain and what data and behaviors they have. C++ supports both paradigms, which is one reason it remains widely used.

images.description: Image of colorful Lego blocks representing reusable building blocks, analogous to how classes and objects serve as reusable components in object-oriented programming.

title: Exercise: Decomposing into Functions vs Objects
summary: To decompose into functions, list verbs/tasks. To decompose into objects, listen for nouns, objects, or agents that interact.
main_text: To decompose a program into functions, try listing the verbs or tasks that are performed to solve the problem. For example, model a card game as a series of tasks or procedures, or consider a database representing a social network. To decompose a program into objects, listen for the nouns, objects, or agents that are interacting. This distinction is key: procedural decomposition focuses on actions (what does the program do?), while object-oriented decomposition focuses on entities (what things exist in the problem?).
notes_text: This exercise helps students develop the mental shift from procedural to object-oriented thinking. In a card game example, the procedural approach would identify tasks like shuffle, deal, draw, and play. The object-oriented approach would identify objects like Deck, Card, Player, and Hand. Both approaches can solve the same problem, but object-oriented design often scales better for complex systems.

title: Object-Oriented Approach: Encapsulation and Abstraction
summary: Objects fuse data and functions into one entity. Encapsulation bundles code and data with controlled access. Abstraction hides implementation details.
main_text: The object-oriented approach models the application or software as a set of objects that interact with each other. Objects fuse data (i.e. variables) and functions (a.k.a methods) that operate on that data into one entity. Objects replace global-level functions as the primary method of encapsulation and abstraction. Encapsulation means code plus data together with controlled access: you group data and code that operates on that data together into one unit, and only expose a well-defined interface to control misuse of the code by other programmers. Abstraction means hiding of data and implementation details: it is how we decompose the problem and think about our design at a higher level rather than considering everything at the lower level.
notes_text: Encapsulation and abstraction are two of the core pillars of object-oriented programming. Encapsulation protects internal state from unauthorized access (like making data members private). Abstraction allows users of an object to interact with it through a simple interface without needing to understand the complex implementation underneath. These concepts will become even more important when studying classes in Unit 5.

title: Focus on the Data: Objects as Collections of Primitives
summary: Objects represent higher-level concepts by aggregating primitive types. Structs in C and classes in C++ bundle different data variables together.
main_text: We want to represent higher level concepts or objects beyond our primitive int, char, or double types. Examples include a pixel, a circle, a student, and a file. These objects can be represented as a collection of primitive types (i.e. as a collection of ints, chars, doubles, or arrays of these). A pixel has a red, green, and blue value (3 numbers). A circle has a radius and a center point (x and y location). A student has a name (string), ID (int), and major (an int/enumeration). Objects (embodied as structs in C and later classes in C++) allow us to aggregate different type data variables together to represent a single larger entity as well as supporting operations (functions) on that data. You can reference the collection with a single name (myCircle, student1) and can access individual components (myCircle.radius, student1.id).
notes_text: This slide motivates why we need structs and classes. Without them, representing a student would require separate variables for name, id, and major that have no formal connection. With a struct, all related data is bundled into a single named entity that can be passed to functions, stored in arrays, and manipulated as a unit.

title: Motivation for Objects: The Suitcase Analogy
summary: Objects bundle related data together like a suitcase bundles luggage, simplifying function signatures and data management.
main_text: When going to the airport, would you rather carry all your luggage items piecemeal or pack everything in one suitcase? This analogy illustrates the motivation for objects. Without objects, passing student data to a function requires listing every field separately: void process(char name[], int id, int major). With objects, you pass a single bundled entity: void process(Student s1). The suitcase diagram shows a Student object s1 containing three data members: name, id, and major, all bundled together. This makes function calls cleaner, reduces errors from mismatched parameters, and keeps related data organized.
notes_text: This is a powerful analogy for understanding why objects exist. Just as a suitcase keeps your belongings organized and easy to transport, a struct keeps related data organized and easy to pass through your program. As objects grow more complex with many data members, the advantage of bundling becomes even more significant.

images.description: Three images showing the analogy: a person carrying loose items (piecemeal approach), a suitcase (bundled approach), and a blue suitcase-like object labeled s1 with compartments for name, id, and major representing a Student struct.

title: Object-Oriented Programming: Data Members and Methods
summary: Objects contain data members (state) and methods/functions (behavior). Example: a Deck of cards object with array data and shuffle/cut methods.
main_text: Objects contain two main components: Data members, which are data needed to model the object and track its state or operation (just like structs), and Methods/Functions, which are code that operates on the object, modifies it, etc. Example: a Deck of cards object would have Data members consisting of an array of 52 entries (one for each card) indicating their ordering and a Top index. Its Methods/Functions would include shuffle(), cut(), and get_top_card(). This shows how objects combine both the data that describes an entity and the operations that can be performed on it.
notes_text: The deck of cards example is excellent for understanding the relationship between data and methods. The data (array of cards, top index) represents the state of the deck at any moment. The methods (shuffle, cut, get_top_card) represent the actions you can perform on that state. This combination of state and behavior is the essence of object-oriented programming.

title: C++ Objects: Structs vs. Classes
summary: Structs originated in C and are predecessors to C++ classes. They are 99.9% identical; both group related data and operations together.
main_text: Structs (originated in the C language) are the predecessors of classes (C++ language). Though structs are still valid in C++ and now behave almost EXACTLY the same as a class (i.e. struct/class are 99.9% THE SAME, with the one difference to be explained later). Classes form the basis of object-oriented programming in the C++ language. Both are simply a way of grouping related data together and related operations (functions or methods) to model some object. We will look at structs now, and classes a bit later, but recall they are interchangeable. Pay attention now to make subsequent lectures easier.
notes_text: The key difference between struct and class in C++ is the default access level: struct members are public by default, while class members are private by default. Otherwise, they are functionally identical. This lecture focuses on structs first because they are simpler and come from C, making them a natural stepping stone to understanding classes.

title: Structs Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing structs as the starting point for learning about data grouping in C++.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the topic of Structs with the subtitle: Starting with data... Structs are the first concrete mechanism introduced for grouping related data variables together in C++.
notes_text: This section will cover struct declaration syntax, instantiation, member access, memory layout, and how structs interact with functions and pointers. Mastering structs is essential before moving on to classes.

title: Structs Overview: Declaration and Instantiation
summary: A struct groups data variables together to represent an abstract concept. It must be declared first (blueprint), then instantiated any number of times.
main_text: A struct allows us to group many data variables together to represent something more abstract. It needs to be declared first (i.e. create a blueprint). This creates a new TYPE in the same way that int and double are a type. Then it can be instantiated any number of times. The code example shows: #include<iostream>, using namespace std; followed by the declaration (blueprint): struct student { char name[80]; int id; int major; }; Then in main: student s1; and student s2; are instantiations that create actual variables of the student type.
notes_text: The declaration vs instantiation distinction is fundamental. The struct declaration (blueprint) tells the compiler what a student looks like but does not allocate any memory. Each instantiation (like student s1;) allocates memory for all the data members. You can create as many instances as needed, each with their own independent copies of the data members.

images.description: Code example showing a struct student declaration with name, id, and major fields, followed by instantiation of s1 and s2 in the main function.

title: Analogy: The Human Body as an Object [1]
summary: The human body illustrates objects: it is a single entity made of smaller data members, with DNA as the blueprint (type) for creating instances.
main_text: The single entity of the human body (an object) is made of many smaller pieces (data members): Arms, Legs, Heart, Brain. Our DNA has the blueprint (the type) but is not an actual human. The blueprint can be used to create many objects/instances (humans). This analogy helps clarify the distinction between a type definition (DNA/blueprint/struct declaration) and an instance (an actual human/variable).
notes_text: This analogy reinforces the type vs instance distinction. Just as DNA contains instructions for building a human but is not itself a human, a struct declaration describes the layout of data but does not create any actual data. Multiple humans can be created from the same DNA blueprint, just as multiple struct instances can be created from the same struct declaration.

images.description: Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man drawing, used to illustrate the human body as an object composed of multiple data members (arms, legs, heart, brain) with DNA serving as the blueprint.

title: Types and Instances: Memory, Meaning, and Operations
summary: A type defines memory requirements, bit interpretation, and supported operations. A variable is an actual instantiation (memory allocation) of a type.
main_text: A type indicates: How much memory will be required, What the bits mean (i.e. integer, double, pointer), and What operations can be performed. For example, int is 32-bits representing only integer values and supporting +, -, *, /, =, ==, <, >, etc. char* is 64-bits representing an address and supporting * (dereference), &, +, - (but not multiply and divide). Types are like blueprints for what and how to make a particular thing. A variable (or object) is an actual instantiation (allocation of memory) for one of these types. Examples: int x, double z, char *str, Student s1, Circle c;
notes_text: This slide connects the concept of types back to primitive types students already know. The key insight is that when you define a struct, you are creating a brand new type with its own memory requirements (the sum of all member sizes), its own meaning (what the grouped data represents), and its own supported operations (initially just assignment). This puts user-defined types on equal footing with built-in types.

title: Definitions and Instances (Declarations): Pixel Struct Example
summary: Objects must be defined as a struct or class first. The definition is a blueprint that creates a new type. Instances are actual objects with allocated memory.
main_text: Objects must first be defined/declared (as a struct or class). The declaration is a blueprint that indicates what any instance should look like. It identifies the overall name of the struct and its individual member types and names. The declaration does not actually create a variable (no memory is allocated). It usually appears outside any function. Once declared, any number of instances can be created/instantiated in your code. Instances are actual objects (memory is allocated for each) created from the definition (blueprint). They are declared like other variables. Example: struct pixel { unsigned char red; unsigned char green; unsigned char blue; }; makes pixel a type just like int. Then pixel p1; and pixel image[256][256]; are instantiations. You can set members: p1.red = 255; p1.blue = p1.green = 0; and use loops to fill an image array.
notes_text: The pixel struct example is particularly good because it shows a practical use case. Each pixel has three color channels (red, green, blue), each stored as an unsigned char (0-255). The example also shows that you can create arrays of structs (pixel image[256][256]) to represent an entire image, demonstrating how structs compose with other data structures.

images.description: Diagram showing a pixel struct with three members (red, green, blue) as adjacent memory slots, alongside code showing struct definition and instantiation of p1 and a 256x256 image array. Arrows indicate the pixel p1 instance with values 255, 0, 0.

title: Memory View of Objects: Student Struct in Memory
summary: Objects can have data members that are arrays or other objects. Memory is allocated contiguously for all members of a struct.
main_text: Objects can have data members that are arrays or even other objects. The code example declares: struct student { char name[80]; int id; int major; }; When student s1; is instantiated, memory is allocated contiguously. Starting at address 7300, s1.name occupies 80 bytes (addresses 7300-7379). At address 7380, s1.id stores the value 1682942 (4 bytes). At address 7384, s1.major stores the value 1 (4 bytes). The total struct occupies 88 bytes of contiguous memory. The name field contains 'J', 'i', 'l', 'l', '\0' followed by uninitialized bytes. Values shown with '?' represent uninitialized memory.
notes_text: Understanding the memory layout of structs is essential for working with pointers to structs and for understanding pass-by-value semantics. The contiguous layout means the address of the struct is the address of its first member. Note that the id value 1682942 shown is arbitrary (uninitialized in this context), illustrating that struct members contain garbage values until explicitly initialized.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the layout of a student struct s1 starting at address 7300. The name field spans addresses 7300-7379 (80 bytes), followed by id at 7380 (4 bytes with value 1682942) and major at 7384 (4 bytes with value 1). Uninitialized bytes are shown with question marks.

title: Membership Operator (.) for Accessing Struct Members
summary: The dot (.) operator accesses individual members of a struct instance using the syntax instance_name.member_name.
main_text: Each variable (and function) in an object definition is called a member of the object (i.e. struct or class). When declaring an instance/variable of an object, we give the entire object a name, but the individual members are identified with the member names provided earlier in the object definition. We use the . (dot/membership) operator to access that member in an instance of the object. Supply the name used in the definition above so that code is in the form: instance_name.member_name. The example shows: enum {CSCI=1, CECS=2}; struct student { char name[80]; int id; int major; }; Then in main: student my_student; my_student.id = 1682942; my_student.major = CSCI; The diagram shows the my_student object as a suitcase-like container with compartments for name ("Jill"), id (1682942), and major (1).
notes_text: The dot operator is one of the most frequently used operators when working with structs and classes. It connects an instance name on the left with a member name on the right. Note that you cannot use the member name alone (like id = 5) because the compiler does not know which instance you mean. You must always specify the instance: my_student.id = 5.

images.description: Suitcase diagram showing the my_student struct instance with three labeled compartments: name containing 'Jill', id containing 1682942, and major containing 1. Code example shows accessing members with the dot operator.

title: Analogy: The Human Body [2] - Using Specific Instances
summary: You cannot command a blueprint; you must use a specific instance. Use s1.id, not student.id, to access members of a particular object.
main_text: We cannot command the blueprint to do anything. It is abstract. We do not say 'Human, move your arm.' Similarly, do not say student.id. We say 'Tommy, move your arm.' Similarly, say s1.id. We need to use a SPECIFIC object. The code example shows: student s1; strcpy(s1.name, "Tommy"); s1.id = 1682942; s1.major = CSCI; This reinforces that you always access members through a specific instance, never through the type name itself.
notes_text: This analogy drives home the type vs instance distinction one more time. Just as you cannot tell the concept of a human to do something (you must address a specific person), you cannot access data through a struct type name. You must have a concrete instance. This is a common mistake for beginners who try to write student.name instead of s1.name.

images.description: Vitruvian Man drawing alongside code showing a student struct instantiation s1 with name set to Tommy, id to 1682942, and major to CSCI, illustrating that you must operate on specific instances rather than blueprints.

title: Important Notes About Objects Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing assignment semantics and pointers to objects.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing Important Notes About Objects, covering assignment semantics and pointers to objects. These are critical concepts for understanding how structs behave when copied, passed to functions, and accessed through pointers.
notes_text: This section covers practical mechanics that students must understand to use structs correctly: how assignment copies all members, what operators are NOT automatically available, and how to use pointers with structs including the arrow operator.

title: Object Assignment: Initializing Struct Members
summary: Shows the initialization of a student struct s1 with strncpy for name, and direct assignment for id and major, with memory layout.
main_text: Consider the following initialization of s1: student s1, s2; strncpy(s1.name, "Jill", 80); s1.id = 5; s1.major = CECS; The memory layout shows s1 starting at address 7300. s1.name begins at 7300 with 'J', 'i', 'l', 'l', '\0' followed by uninitialized bytes through address 7379. s1.id at address 7380 contains the value 5. s1.major at address 7384 contains the value 2 (CECS). The s2 variable follows in memory at addresses 7388 and beyond, with all values uninitialized (shown as question marks).
notes_text: This slide sets up the scenario for the next slide which demonstrates object assignment. Note the use of strncpy instead of strcpy for safety, and the use of the CECS enum value which equals 2. The memory diagram helps students visualize exactly where each piece of data lives in memory.

images.description: Memory diagram showing struct s1 at addresses 7300-7384 with name='Jill', id=5, major=2, followed by uninitialized s2 memory from address 7388 onward.

title: Object Assignment: Member-by-Member Copy
summary: Assigning one struct to another (s2 = s1) performs a member-by-member copy of all data from the source to the destination object.
main_text: Assigning one object to another will perform a member-by-member copy of the entire source object to the destination object. When s2 = s1; is executed, every byte of s1 is copied into s2. The memory diagram shows that after assignment, s2.name at address 7388 contains 'J', 'i', 'l', 'l', '\0', s2.id at address 7408 contains 1682942, and s2.major at address 7412 contains 2, all matching s1's values exactly. Yellow arrows indicate data flowing from s1's name, id, and major fields down into s2's corresponding fields. Normally, C/C++ perform only one operation at a time and make you write code if you want to do more. But object assignment is an exception (probably because we cannot loop through the different members of a struct).
notes_text: The member-by-member copy is also called a shallow copy. For structs containing only primitive types and fixed-size arrays (like char name[80]), this works perfectly because all data is contained within the struct itself. However, if a struct contains pointers to dynamically allocated memory, a shallow copy only copies the pointer value (address), not the pointed-to data. This distinction becomes important later when studying deep vs shallow copies.

images.description: Memory diagram showing s1 and s2 struct instances with yellow arrows indicating the member-by-member copy from s1 to s2. Both suitcase-like objects show identical contents after the assignment operation. Memory addresses show s1 at 7300-7384 and s2 at 7388-7412.

title: Object Operators - No Free Lunch
summary: The assignment (=) operator is the ONLY operator automatically defined for structs. Comparison (==), output (<<), and input (>>) do NOT work by default.
main_text: The assignment (=) operation is the ONLY one the compiler will define automatically for a struct or class. It does NOT allow you to compare objects (==, <, >). It does NOT allow you to print objects or get input to a full object (cout << object or cin >> object). The = operator is the only one you get for free! The code example shows that after defining a student struct and performing s2 = s1 (which works), attempting cout << s2 or if(s1 == s2) will fail to compile. A prohibition symbol is shown next to these invalid operations.
notes_text: This is a critical rule that students must internalize. Unlike primitive types where all common operators work, user-defined types only get assignment automatically. To enable other operations, you must write custom operator overloads, which is covered later in the course. For now, to compare or print struct data, you must access individual members explicitly.

images.description: Code example showing valid assignment (s2 = s1) and invalid operations (cout << s2 and if(s1 == s2)) marked with a red prohibition circle, illustrating that only = works automatically for structs.

title: Passing Objects as Arguments: Pass-by-Value
summary: Structs are passed by value to functions, making a member-by-member copy. Use pointers for large objects to avoid expensive copies.
main_text: We can pass entire objects to a function but since they are one entity (and not an array), they are passed-by-value. The copy is made member-by-member. Of course, you can always pass a pointer (especially for big objects since pass by value means making a copy of a large object). The example shows: struct Point { int x; int y; }; void print_point(Point myp) { cout << "(x,y)=" << myp.x << "," << myp.y; cout << endl; } In main: Point p1; p1.x = 2; p1.y = 5; print_point(p1); The diagram shows p1 with values x=2, y=5 being copied member-by-member into myp with the same values x=2, y=5.
notes_text: This is an important distinction from arrays, which are always passed by reference (as a pointer to the first element). Structs behave like individual variables and are copied entirely when passed to functions. For small structs like Point (8 bytes), this is fine. For large structs like student (88 bytes), the copy overhead may be significant, making pointer passing more efficient.

images.description: Diagram showing two suitcase-like objects: p1 (with x=2, y=5) and myp (with x=2, y=5), connected by yellow arrows indicating the member-by-member copy that occurs when p1 is passed by value to the print_point function.

title: Returning Objects from Functions
summary: Functions can return structs by value, creating a copy of the local struct that is returned to the caller.
main_text: We can also have a struct or class as the return type from a function. It will return a copy of the struct indicated, i.e. return-by-value. The example shows: struct Point { int x; int y; }; Point make_point() { Point temp; temp.x = 3; temp.y = -1; return temp; } In main: Point p1; p1 = make_point(); print_point(&p1); The diagram shows temp (x=3, y=-1) being created inside make_point, then its values being copied down into p1 (x=3, y=-1) via yellow arrows when the function returns.
notes_text: Return by value for structs works the same as for primitive types: the local variable is copied to the caller's variable. Modern compilers often optimize this with Return Value Optimization (RVO), eliminating the copy. Note that print_point is called with &p1, passing the address of p1, suggesting it accepts a Point pointer this time for efficiency.

images.description: Diagram showing the temp variable (x=3, y=-1) inside make_point being copied via yellow arrows into p1 (x=3, y=-1) in the calling function, illustrating return-by-value for structs.

title: Pointers to Objects
summary: Pointers to structs work like pointers to any other variable. The address of a struct is its starting memory address.
main_text: We can declare pointers to objects just as any other variable. The address of a struct is just (you guessed it) its starting address. The example shows: student s1; student *sptr; sptr = &s1; The memory diagram shows sptr at addresses 7388-7392 containing the value 7300 (the address of s1). s1 starts at address 7300 with s1.name, has s1.id at 7380 with value 5, and s1.major at 7384 with value 2. A curved arrow from sptr points to the beginning of s1 at address 7300, labeled &s1.
notes_text: Pointers to structs are essential for two primary use cases: passing structs by reference to functions (to avoid copies and to allow modification of the original) and dynamic allocation of structs with new. The address of a struct is simply the address of its first byte in memory, which is the same as the address of its first member.

images.description: Memory diagram showing sptr variable storing address 7300 (as two 4-byte values 0x00007300), with a curved arrow pointing to the start of s1 at address 7300. The s1 struct layout shows name, id=5, and major=2.

title: Why Pointers To Objects? Pass-by-Reference and Dynamic Allocation
summary: Pointers to objects enable pass-by-reference and dynamic allocation. The dot operator has higher precedence than dereference, requiring parentheses.
main_text: We use pointers to objects for the same reasons we want pointers to variables: Pass-by-reference and dynamic allocation. But there is a nasty precedence (order of operations) issue when we dereference. The example shows: void init(student *sptr){ strncpy((*sptr).name, "Jill", 80); (*sptr).id = 5; (*sptr).major = CECS; } int main(){ student s1; init(&s1); cout << s1.name << endl; return 0; } The memory diagram shows sptr at addresses 7292-7296 pointing to s1 at address 7300, with s1.name containing 'Jill', s1.id = 5, and s1.major = 2.
notes_text: The precedence issue is important: the dot operator (.) has higher precedence than the dereference operator (*). So *sptr.name would be interpreted as *(sptr.name), trying to apply dot to a pointer, which is wrong. You must write (*sptr).name to first dereference the pointer, then access the member. This cumbersome syntax motivates the arrow operator introduced next.

images.description: Memory diagram showing sptr pointer at address 7292 pointing to s1 at address 7300, with the complete student struct layout. Code shows the init function using (*sptr).member syntax to access struct members through a pointer.

title: Accessing Members and Dereferencing: Precedence Problem
summary: The dot operator has higher precedence than the dereference operator, requiring (*structptr).member syntax which is verbose and error-prone.
main_text: Sadly, the dot operator (.) has higher precedence than the dereference operator (*), requiring you to use parentheses. So, you'd have to write (*structptr).member rather than *structptr.member. This is too much! The code example shows the same init function: void init(student *sptr){ strncpy((*sptr).name, "Jill", 80); (*sptr).id = 5; (*sptr).major = CECS; } And main calling init(&s1); and printing s1.name. The memory diagram reiterates sptr at address 7292-7296 pointing to s1 at 7300.
notes_text: This slide emphasizes the inconvenience of the (*ptr).member syntax to motivate the arrow operator on the next slide. Without parentheses, *sptr.name would try to apply the dot operator to sptr first (which is a pointer, not a struct), causing a compilation error. The parentheses force dereference to happen first, yielding the struct, then dot accesses the member.

images.description: Memory diagram identical to previous slide, reinforcing the sptr to s1 pointer relationship and the need for parentheses in (*sptr).member syntax.

title: Arrow (->) Operator for Pointer-to-Member Access
summary: The arrow operator (->) combines dereference and member access: (*struct_ptr).member is equivalent to struct_ptr->member.
main_text: Save keystrokes and have cleaner looking code by using the arrow (->) operator. (*struct_ptr).member is equivalent to struct_ptr->member. Always have a pointer on the left of the -> and a member on the right. The example shows: void init(student *sptr){ strncpy(sptr->name, "Jill", 80); sptr->id = 5; sptr->major = CECS; } int main(){ student s1; init(&s1); cout << s1.name << endl; return 0; } This is much cleaner than using (*sptr).name, (*sptr).id, and (*sptr).major.
notes_text: The arrow operator is one of the most commonly used operators in C and C++ when working with dynamically allocated objects or when passing objects by pointer. The rule is simple: use dot (.) when you have a struct variable, use arrow (->) when you have a pointer to a struct. This will be used extensively throughout the rest of the course.

images.description: Memory diagram showing sptr pointing to s1, with code using the clean arrow operator syntax (sptr->name, sptr->id, sptr->major) instead of the verbose (*sptr).member syntax.

title: Dynamically Allocating Objects with new
summary: Structs can be dynamically allocated using new, returning a pointer. Use the arrow operator to access members and delete to free memory.
main_text: The example demonstrates dynamic allocation of a student struct. The function makeStudent takes parameters and creates a new student on the heap: student* makeStudent(const char* n, int i, int m) { student* stuptr = new student; strcpy(stuptr->name, n, 80); stuptr->id = i; stuptr->major = m; return stuptr; } In main: student* stuptr = makeStudent("Jane Doe", 5, CECS); cout << stuptr->name << endl; (prints "Jane Doe"). Then delete stuptr; frees the memory. The memory diagram shows the new student allocated on the heap starting at address 7300 with name="Jane Doe", id=5, major=2, and stuptr at address 7388 pointing to 7300.
notes_text: Dynamic allocation of structs is essential when you do not know at compile time how many objects you need, or when objects must persist beyond the scope of the function that creates them. The makeStudent function creates an object on the heap and returns a pointer to it. The caller is responsible for calling delete to free the memory when done. Failing to delete causes a memory leak.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a dynamically allocated student struct on the heap at address 7300 (name='Jane Doe', id=5, major=2) with stuptr at address 7388 pointing to it via a curved arrow.

title: Returning Objects: Using Pointers with Arrow Operator
summary: Functions can return structs by value. When accepting pointers to objects, use the arrow operator (->) to access members.
main_text: This slide revisits returning objects but now uses pointer syntax for the print function. struct Point { int x; int y; }; void print_point(Point *myp) { cout << "(x,y)=" << myp->x << "," << myp->y; cout << endl; } Point make_point() { Point temp; temp.x = 3; temp.y = -1; return temp; } int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { Point p1; p1 = make_point(); print_point(&p1); return 0; } The print_point function now takes a Point pointer and uses the arrow operator (myp->x, myp->y) to access members, while make_point returns by value.
notes_text: This combined example shows both patterns: returning by value (make_point returns a Point copy) and passing by pointer (print_point takes Point*). Passing by pointer is more efficient for large structs since no copy is made. For a small struct like Point (8 bytes), the efficiency difference is negligible, but the pattern is important for larger objects.

images.description: Diagram showing temp struct (x=3, y=-1) in make_point being copied to p1, then p1's address being passed to print_point which uses arrow operator to access members.

title: C++ Strings Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing C++ strings as the next major topic after structs.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the topic of C++ Strings. After learning about structs, the lecture transitions to C++ strings as a practical example of a useful object provided by the C++ standard library.
notes_text: C++ strings are presented here because they are an excellent real-world example of an object that students will use frequently. The string class demonstrates encapsulation and abstraction in action: it hides the complexity of character array management behind a clean interface.

title: Motivation for C++ Strings
summary: Before writing custom objects, learn to use objects from the C++ library. The string class is one of the most basic and useful library objects.
main_text: Before we dive deeper into writing our OWN objects, let's learn how to use objects (structs/classes) that the C++ library already provides us. One of the most basic (and useful) objects in the C++ library is the string class. To understand what they do for you (and how they provide encapsulation and abstraction), let's review how we dealt with strings in C (i.e. before the string class existed).
notes_text: This motivational slide frames C++ strings as a practical application of the object-oriented concepts just covered. Students will see how the string class encapsulates character array management (memory allocation, deep copying, null termination) and abstracts these details behind simple operators like =, +, and ==.

title: Review: C Strings (Character Arrays)
summary: In C, strings are character arrays terminated with NULL, passed by pointer, require care for copies (shallow vs deep), and use the cstring library.
main_text: In C, strings are: Character arrays (char mystring[80];), Terminated with a NULL character ('\0' which equals 0), Passed by reference/pointer (char *) to functions, Require care when making copies with the distinction between Shallow (only copying the pointer) vs. Deep (copying the entire array of characters), and are Processed using the C String library (<cstring>).
notes_text: This review of C strings sets up the contrast with C++ strings. Every limitation listed here (fixed size, manual null termination, pointer semantics, explicit deep copy, reliance on library functions) will be addressed by the C++ string class. Students who struggled with C strings will appreciate how C++ strings simplify these operations.

title: Review: C-String Library (cstring) Functions
summary: Key cstring functions: strlen for length, strcmp for comparison, strcpy/strncpy for copying, strcat/strncat for concatenation, strchr for character search.
main_text: In C, we have to pass a C-String as an argument for the function to operate on it. Key functions: int strlen(char *dest) returns the string length. int strcmp(char *str1, char *str2) returns 0 if equal, >0 if first non-equal char in str1 is alphanumerically larger, <0 otherwise. char *strcpy(char *dest, char *src) copies src to dest. strncpy(char *dest, char *src, int n) copies maximum of n characters. char *strcat(char *dest, char *src) concatenates src onto dest. strncat(char *dest, char *src, int n) concatenates maximum of n characters plus a NULL. char *strchr(char *str, char c) finds first occurrence of character c in str, returning a pointer to that character or NULL if not found. Example of danger: strcpy(temp_buf, str) where temp_buf is only 5 chars but str is "Too much" causes a buffer overflow.
notes_text: These C string functions are error-prone because they provide no bounds checking by default. strcpy and strcat are particularly dangerous because they will write past the end of the destination buffer if it is too small. The 'n' variants (strncpy, strncat) add safety by limiting the number of characters, but require the programmer to calculate sizes correctly. This complexity motivates the C++ string class.

images.description: Code example showing a dangerous strcpy call where a 5-character temp_buf receives the string 'Too much', demonstrating a buffer overflow scenario.

title: Review: Shallow vs. Deep C-String Copy
summary: Using assignment with char* arrays creates shallow copies (all pointers share one buffer). Must allocate new storage for deep copies.
main_text: Recall the conversation about shallow vs. deep copies. Can we just use the assignment operator '=' with character arrays? No, must allocate new storage. The example shows storing 10 user names using char* names[10] and a single char temp_buf[40] as a scratchpad. In a loop: cin >> temp_buf; names[i] = temp_buf; This creates a shallow copy where all 10 names[i] pointers point to the same temp_buf address (2000). Every entry ends up containing the last input because they all point to the same memory. The correct approach requires dynamically allocating separate storage for each name and using strcpy. Memory must also be freed: for(int i=0; i < 10; i++){ delete [] names[i]; }
notes_text: This is a classic pitfall with C strings. The assignment operator for pointers copies the address, not the data. All 10 entries in the names array end up pointing to the same temp_buf, so they all show the last value entered. Understanding this problem is essential for appreciating why C++ strings automatically perform deep copies when assigned.

images.description: Diagram showing 10 char* pointers in the names array all pointing to the same myInput buffer at address 2000, illustrating the shallow copy problem where all entries share one buffer.

title: Review: Deep Copies - Three Required Steps
summary: A deep copy requires three steps: determine size, dynamically allocate memory, and explicitly copy the data using strcpy or a loop.
main_text: A deep copy usually requires 3 steps: Determine the size of the data to copy (if it is not known), Dynamic allocation of an array of that size, and Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). The corrected code shows: char* names[10]; char myInput[40]; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++){ cin >> myInput; int len = strlen(myInput); names[i] = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(names[i], myInput); } Now names[0] at address 2130 points to 'Ti\0', names[1] at address 2610 points to 'Christopher\0', each with their own independently allocated memory.
notes_text: The three-step deep copy pattern (measure, allocate, copy) is fundamental in C programming and applies beyond strings to any dynamically managed data. The +1 in new char[len + 1] is critical to allocate space for the null terminator. C++ strings eliminate all three steps by handling them automatically in the assignment operator.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names array with each entry pointing to independently allocated character arrays: names[0] at 2130 pointing to 'Ti\0', names[1] at 2610 pointing to 'Christopher\0', illustrating proper deep copies.

title: C++ Strings: Abstraction and Encapsulation in Action
summary: The C++ string class abstracts memory management, deep copying, concatenation, comparison, and size tracking, encapsulating all the complexity.
main_text: So, you don't like remembering all these details? You can do it! Don't give up. C++ provides a string class that abstracts all those worrisome details and encapsulates all the code to actually handle: Memory allocation and sizing, Deep copy, Concatenation, Comparison, Size information, etc. The string class is a perfect example of how objects simplify programming by hiding complex implementation details behind a clean, easy-to-use interface.
notes_text: This slide is the bridge between the C string pain points and the C++ string solutions. Every difficulty discussed in the previous slides (manual memory allocation, buffer overflow risk, shallow copy bugs, strcmp for comparison, strcat for concatenation) is handled automatically by the string class. This is the power of encapsulation and abstraction.

title: C-Strings vs C++ Strings: Side-by-Side Comparison
summary: C strings are null-terminated char arrays using cstring functions. C++ strings (std::string) are objects that manage memory automatically with a size and data pointer.
main_text: C Strings (char *) are null-terminated character arrays. You must use functions from the <cstring> library to perform nearly all manipulations. Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; creates a character array at address 2000 with 'J','a','n','e','\0' followed by unused bytes up to index 19. C++ Strings (std::string) are a C++ class/object that gives a simplified interface that allocates/deallocates memory for you and calls all the <cstring> functions behind the scenes. Example: string s2 = "Jane"; creates a string object with two internal data members: an int size (value 4) and a char* data pointer (value 2000) pointing to a dynamically allocated array containing 'J','a','n','e','\0'. Behind the scenes, the string constructor calls: size = strlen(myInput); data = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(data, myInput);
notes_text: This side-by-side comparison clearly shows how the string class wraps a C string with additional metadata (size) and automatic memory management. The string object internally maintains a pointer to a dynamically allocated character array, just like what you would have to do manually with C strings. The key difference is that all this management is automatic.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison diagram. Left: C string s1 as a char array at address 2000 with fixed size 20. Right: C++ string s2 as an object with int size=4 and char* data=2000 pointing to a dynamically allocated 'Jane\0' array. Bottom shows the internal operations the string constructor performs.

title: String Declaration: C vs C++ Comparison
summary: C strings require a fixed size at declaration. C++ strings need no size; they manage memory automatically, acting as both a single variable and a dynamic array.
main_text: C Strings: Must give it a size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; creates a char array at address 2000 with 'J','a','n','e','\0' and unused space up to index 19. C++ Strings: No size necessary. Is it an array or a single variable? Yes! (huh?) Example: string s2 = "Jane"; creates a string object with int size=4 and char* data=2000 pointing to a dynamically allocated array containing 'J','a','n','e','\0'. The C++ string handles memory sizing automatically.
notes_text: The 'Is it an array or a single variable? Yes!' comment highlights that a C++ string is a single object variable that internally manages a dynamic array. This duality is the essence of encapsulation: from the outside it looks like a simple variable, but inside it manages a complex data structure.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of C string declaration (char s1[20] with fixed 20-byte array) and C++ string declaration (string s2 with automatic sizing), showing internal memory representations.

title: Array Indexing Ability: C vs C++ Strings
summary: Both C and C++ strings support square bracket indexing to access/change individual characters, despite C++ strings being objects rather than arrays.
main_text: C Strings: Treat it like an array (since it is) and access/change individual elements using square bracket [] (indexing operation). Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; s1[2] = 'k'; changes 'n' to 'k', making s1 contain 'J','a','k','e','\0'. C++ Strings: Treat it like an array (though it is NOT) and access/change individual elements using square bracket [] (indexing operation). Example: string s2 = "Jane"; s2[2] = 'k'; similarly changes the string to 'Jake'. The size member remains 4, and data still points to the character array.
notes_text: The fact that C++ strings support [] indexing is an example of operator overloading: the string class defines what [] means for string objects, making them behave like arrays even though they are objects. This demonstrates how C++ classes can provide intuitive interfaces that feel natural to programmers familiar with C-style arrays.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing both C string s1 and C++ string s2 being indexed with [2] to change 'n' to 'k', transforming 'Jane' to 'Jake' in both cases.

title: Printing Strings with cout
summary: Both C and C++ strings can be printed with cout. Both have a special relationship with the << operator for outputting the full string.
main_text: C Strings: Print the WHOLE string with cout (remember the special relationship it has with char*). Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; cout << s1 << endl; outputs 'Jane'. C++ Strings: Print the WHOLE string with cout (It, too, has a special relationship). Example: string s2 = "Jane"; cout << s2 << endl; also outputs 'Jane'. Both behave identically when printed with cout, producing the expected string output.
notes_text: For C strings, cout knows to print characters until it encounters a null terminator when given a char*. For C++ strings, the << operator has been overloaded to print the string contents. Despite different internal mechanisms, the user experience is identical, demonstrating good abstraction.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing cout << s1 and cout << s2 both producing 'Jane' as terminal output, with memory diagrams of each string type.

title: Input with cin: Fixed vs Dynamic Size
summary: C strings overflow if input exceeds array size (BAD THINGS HAPPEN). C++ strings grow automatically to accommodate any input length.
main_text: C Strings: Input a string with cin. Stops at whitespace. BAD THINGS HAPPEN if you type too much due to the array's fixed size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; cin >> s1; If the user types 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxz hello', the 26-character input overflows the 20-character array, writing past the end of s1 into adjacent memory. C++ Strings: Input a string with cin. Stops at whitespace. CAN GROW automatically (think VLA from HW2) as you enter text! Example: string s2 = "Jane"; cin >> s2; With the same input, the string object grows: size updates to 26, data points to a newly allocated array containing all 26 characters plus null terminator. No overflow occurs.
notes_text: This is one of the most compelling advantages of C++ strings over C strings. Buffer overflow is a major security vulnerability in C programs, and cin >> with a fixed-size char array is a common source of this problem. C++ strings eliminate this risk entirely by dynamically resizing their internal buffer. Note that both stop reading at whitespace.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing input overflow in C strings (26 chars overflowing a 20-char array with data spilling into adjacent memory shown in red) versus safe dynamic growth in C++ strings (size updates to 26, data points to properly sized new array).

title: String Length / Size: O(n) vs O(1)
summary: C strings use strlen() which runs in O(n) time. C++ strings store size internally, so .size() or .length() runs in O(1) time.
main_text: C Strings: Does NOT know its size. Have to use strlen() function. Runs in O(n) where n is the string length, because it must scan for the null terminator. Example: char s1[20]; cin >> s1; int len = strlen(s1); With input 'TommyTrojan', len = 11. C++ Strings: Remembers its size! Just call the .size() or .length() method. Runs in O(1) because the size is stored as a data member. Example: string s2; cin >> s2; int len = s2.size(); With the same input, len = 11. The string object shows size=11 and data pointing to 'TommyTrojan\0'.
notes_text: The O(n) vs O(1) performance difference is significant in loops that repeatedly check string length. With C strings, calling strlen() in a loop condition like for(int i=0; i < strlen(s1); i++) recalculates the length every iteration, making the loop O(n^2). With C++ strings, s2.size() is constant time, keeping the loop O(n).

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string requiring strlen() (O(n) scan) versus C++ string using .size() (O(1) member lookup), both returning 11 for 'TommyTrojan'.

title: String Assignment: strcpy vs = Operator
summary: C strings cannot use = after declaration; must use strcpy. C++ strings support = which automatically performs deep copy with dynamic resizing.
main_text: C Strings: Assign one string to another. Cannot assign a new string after declaration. Would have to use strcpy(). MUST ensure you don't copy more than the array size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; char s3[6] = "Maria"; s1 = s3; does NOT work. Must use strcpy(s1, s3); and strcpy(s1, "abcde...wxyz"); but if the source exceeds 20 characters, overflow occurs. C++ Strings: Assign one string to another. CAN GROW automatically as you enter text via a DEEP COPY! Example: string s2 = "Jane"; string s4 = "Maria"; s2 = s4; works perfectly. s2 = "abcde...wxyz"; also works. The string internally deallocates old memory, allocates new memory of the right size, and copies the data. The diagram shows size changing from 4 to 5 to 26 and data pointer updating accordingly, with old arrays being freed.
notes_text: This is a critical difference. C strings cannot use the = operator for assignment after declaration because arrays are not assignable in C/C++. The C++ string class overloads the = operator to perform a proper deep copy: it frees the old internal array, calculates the new size, allocates a new array, and copies the data. This eliminates an entire class of bugs.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string assignment requiring strcpy (with overflow risk marked in red) versus C++ string assignment using = operator with automatic deep copy. The C++ side shows the string object updating its size and data pointer, with old allocations being freed.

title: String Concatenation: strcat vs + Operator
summary: C strings require strcat() for concatenation with overflow risk. C++ strings use the + or += operator with automatic memory growth.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT concatenate/append another string. Cannot use '+' to append a new string except through strcat(). MUST ensure you don't copy more than the array size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; char s3[5] = " Doe"; s1 += s3; does NOT work. Must use strcat(s1, s3); resulting in s1 containing 'J','a','n','e',' ','D','o','e','\0'. C++ Strings: Can concatenate/append easily (with + op). Can use '+' to append. CAN GROW automatically via a DEEP COPY! Example: string s2 = "Jane"; string s4 = " Doe"; s2 += s4; The string object updates: size changes from 4 to 8, data is reallocated to point to a new array containing 'Jane Doe\0', and the old 'Jane\0' array is freed.
notes_text: Concatenation highlights another major advantage of C++ strings. With C strings, strcat has no bounds checking and can easily overflow. With C++ strings, += performs the necessary steps automatically: allocate new memory large enough for both strings, copy the combined content, free the old memory. The + operator can also be used to create a new string: string s5 = s2 + s4;

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string concatenation with strcat (fixed array, overflow risk) versus C++ string concatenation with += (automatic reallocation from size 4 to 8, old memory freed).

title: String Comparison: strcmp vs ==, <, > Operators
summary: C strings cannot use ==, <, > directly; must use strcmp(). C++ strings support all comparison operators directly with lexicographic ordering.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT compare C-strings directly. Would have to use strcmp(). Example: char s1[20] = "abc"; char s3[5] = "aba"; if(s1 == s3){} and if(s1 > s3){} do NOT work (they compare pointer addresses, not string content). Must use: if(strcmp(s1,s3) == 0) {} which is false, and if(strcmp(s1,s3) == 1) {} which is true (since 'c' > 'a'). C++ Strings: Can use basic ==, <, > operators to compare! Example: string s2 = "abc"; string s4 = "aba"; if(s2 == s4) {} is false. if(s2 > s4) {} is true. Comparison is lexicographic (dictionary order).
notes_text: When comparing C strings with == or <, you are comparing the pointer addresses, not the string contents, which almost never gives the result you want. C++ string comparison operators perform character-by-character lexicographic comparison automatically. Lexicographic comparison compares characters left to right; the first difference determines the result. If all compared characters match, the shorter string is considered less than the longer one.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string comparison attempts that fail (comparing addresses) versus C++ string comparisons that work correctly with ==, <, > operators.

title: Conversion to Numerics: atoi/atof vs stoi/stod
summary: Neither C nor C++ strings can be cast to numeric types. C uses atoi()/atof(), while C++ uses stoi()/stod(). C++ also provides to_string() for reverse conversion.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT cast to numeric types. Use atoi() and atof(). Example: char s1[20] = "123.67"; char s3[5] = "42"; double x = (double) s1; does NOT work. int y = (int) s3; does NOT work. Must use: double x = atof(s1); and int y = atoi(s3); C++ Strings: Also, CANNOT cast to numeric types! Use stoi() and stod(). Example: string s2 = "abc"; string s4 = "aba"; double x = (double) s2; does NOT work. int y = (int) s4; does NOT work. Must use: double x = stod(s2); int y = stoi(s4); Additionally, string s6 = to_string(y); converts a number back to a string.
notes_text: The conversion functions are important for parsing user input and file data. atoi/atof (ASCII to integer/float) are C functions. stoi/stod (string to integer/double) are C++11 functions that work with std::string objects. to_string() is the reverse operation, available since C++11. Note that stoi/stod will throw exceptions on invalid input, which is safer than atoi/atof which return 0 on failure.

title: String Documentation and Other Functions: size(), substr()
summary: Use the dot operator to call string member functions. Key functions include .size() for length and .substr() for extracting substrings.
main_text: Use the dot operator to call an operation (function) on an object or access a data value. Asking for the string size: call the .size() function on a string to get the number of characters stored in the string. Can generate substrings by calling either of the 2 versions: .substr(start_index) or .substr(start_index, length) function on the string. Many more member functions are available at http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/string/string/. Example: string mystr = "CS 103"; cout << mystr.size() << endl; outputs 6. string s = mystr.substr(2); gives s = "103". mystr = "Computer Science"; cout << mystr.size() << endl; outputs 16. s = mystr.substr(9,2); gives s = "Sc".
notes_text: The .substr() function is very useful for string parsing. With one argument, it returns everything from the start index to the end. With two arguments, it returns 'length' characters starting from start_index. These are member functions called with the dot operator on a string instance, demonstrating the object-oriented pattern of invoking operations on objects.

images.description: Code example showing string member function usage: .size() returning 6 for 'CS 103' and 16 for 'Computer Science', and .substr() extracting '103' and 'Sc' from different strings.

title: Other Member Functions: c_str(), find(), replace, rfind
summary: c_str() converts to C string. find() searches for substrings returning the index or string::npos. Other functions include replace and rfind.
main_text: Get C String (char *) equivalent using .c_str(). Find a substring: Searches for occurrence of a substring. Returns either the index where the substring starts or string::npos. std::npos is a constant meaning 'just beyond the end of the string', a way of saying 'Not found'. Others: replace, rfind, etc. Example: string s1("abcdef"); char my_c_str[80]; strcpy(my_c_str, s1.c_str()); cout << my_c_str << endl; outputs 'abcdef'. size_t idx = s1.find("bcd"); if(idx != string::npos){ cout << "Found bcd starting at pos="; cout << idx << endl; } else { cout << "Not found" << endl; } Output: abcdef, Found bcd starting at pos=1.
notes_text: The .c_str() function is essential for interoperability between C++ strings and C functions that expect char*. The .find() function performs substring search and returns the starting index, or string::npos if not found. Always check against string::npos before using the returned index. rfind() searches from the end of the string backward.

images.description: Code example demonstrating c_str() for C string conversion and find() for substring search, with output showing 'abcdef' and 'Found bcd starting at pos=1'.
labels: Output: Found bcd starting at pos=1

title: String to Number Conversion: to_string, stoi, stod
summary: Casting does NOT work for string-numeric conversion. Use to_string() for number-to-string and stoi()/stod() for string-to-number, available since C++11.
main_text: Recall: Casting does NOT work for string to numeric conversions. Instead, use functions defined in <string>. Conversion from number to string: string to_string(int); and string to_string(double); Conversion from string to number: int stoi(string); unsigned int stoul(string); double stod(string); Example code: double a = 3.6; int b = static_cast<int>(a) / 2; works (b = 1, casts 3.6 to 3). int c = 123; string d = static_cast<string>(c); does NOT compile. string d = to_string(c); works (since C++11). string e = "42"; int f = static_cast<int>(e); does NOT compile. int f = stoi(e); works (string-to-int, since C++11). Use stod() for string-to-double.
notes_text: static_cast works between compatible numeric types (int to double, double to int) but does NOT work between strings and numbers because they are fundamentally different types. The to_string/stoi/stod functions perform the actual parsing and formatting needed for conversion. These functions were added in C++11 and are now standard. stoi throws std::invalid_argument if the string does not contain a valid number.

images.description: Code example demonstrating valid and invalid conversions: static_cast works for numeric types, fails for string-numeric. to_string() and stoi()/stod() are the correct approaches for string-numeric conversion.

title: Exercises (If Time Allows)
summary: Practice exercises on palindrome checking and circular shift string operations for reinforcing string manipulation concepts.
main_text: Two exercises are suggested if time allows: Palindrome (checking if a string reads the same forwards and backwards) and Circular Shift (rotating characters in a string). These exercises provide hands-on practice with the string operations covered in this unit.
notes_text: Palindrome checking exercises .size(), [] indexing, and loop construction. A circular shift involves moving characters: for example, 'abcd' shifted left by 1 becomes 'bcda'. Both exercises reinforce understanding of string indexing, .size(), .substr(), and concatenation.

title: Backup Section Header
summary: Section divider for backup/supplementary slides that provide additional examples and details.

title: Memory View of Objects: Pixel Array in Memory (Backup)
summary: Each struct instantiation allocates contiguous memory for all members. A pixel array stores red, green, blue bytes sequentially per element.
main_text: Each instantiation allocates memory for all the members/components of the object (struct or class). The code defines: struct pixel { unsigned char red; unsigned char green; unsigned char blue; }; Then instantiates: pixel p1; pixel image[256][256]; The memory layout at address 0x7400 shows: p1 occupies 3 bytes (red=0x00 at 0x7400, green=0xFF at 0x7401, blue=0x00 at 0x7402). Then image[0][0] starts at 0x7403 (red=0xFF, green=0x00, blue=0x00). image[0][1] starts at 0x7406 (red=0x48, green=0xC9, blue=0x17). Each pixel is exactly 3 bytes, and they are stored contiguously in memory.
notes_text: This backup slide provides a more detailed memory view than the earlier pixel example. The hex values help students connect the abstract concept of struct layout to actual byte-level memory representation. Note that p1 is green (R=0, G=255, B=0), image[0][0] is red (R=255, G=0, B=0), and image[0][1] has specific color values (R=72, G=201, B=23).

images.description: Detailed memory map showing pixel p1 at addresses 0x7400-0x7402 and image array elements at subsequent addresses, with hex values for each byte and labels indicating which pixel and color channel each byte represents.

title: C++ Strings: Do's and Don'ts (Backup)
summary: Key rules for C++ strings: include <string>, initialize with = or constructor, use [] for indexing, use cin/cout, and do not worry about input size.
main_text: In C++, the string class provides an easier alternative to working with plain-old character arrays. Do's and Don'ts: Do #include <string> and put using namespace std; Do initialize using = or by giving an initial value in parentheses (aka use the constructor syntax). Don't need to declare the size (i.e. [7]), just assign. Do still use it like an array by using [index] to get individual characters. Do still use cin/cout with strings. Don't worry about how many characters the user types when inputting to a C++ string. Example: char str1[7] = "CS 103"; (initializes C-style). string str2 = "CS 103"; (initializes C++ string). string str3("Hello"); (constructor syntax). str2[5] = '4'; makes str2 = "CS 104". cout << str2 << endl; prints "CS 104". cin >> str1; (if user types more than 6 chars, uh oh!). cin >> str2; (str2 will adjust to hold whatever the user types).
notes_text: This backup slide serves as a quick reference card for C++ string usage. The most important points are: always include <string>, remember that strings auto-resize so you never specify a size, and you can use the same [] indexing and cin/cout operations you are already familiar with from char arrays.

images.description: Code example showing C++ string declaration, initialization with = and constructor syntax, character modification with [], output with cout, and safe input with cin.

title: What Happens Behind the Scenes: String Internal Operations
summary: Strings internally abstract character arrays. Assignment and concatenation trigger deallocation, reallocation, and copy of the underlying char array.
main_text: Strings simply abstract character arrays. Behind the scenes strings are just creating and manipulating character arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Can concatenate (append) to a string with the + operator. Example: string str2 = "CS 102"; (str2 stores 6 chars = "CS 102"). str2 = "Computer Science"; (now str2 stores 16 characters: the old 'CS 102' array is freed, a new 16-character array is allocated, and 'Computer Science' is copied in). str2 = str2 + " is cool"; (now str2 stores 24 characters: the old 16-char array is freed, a new 24-char array is allocated, and 'Computer Science is cool' is copied in). The string object internally contains a data pointer and a size member. Each reassignment or concatenation may trigger deallocation of old storage and allocation of new storage.
notes_text: Understanding the behind-the-scenes behavior is important for performance awareness. Every time a string grows beyond its current capacity, memory reallocation occurs (which involves allocating new memory, copying all characters, and freeing old memory). This is why repeatedly concatenating in a loop can be slow. In practice, string implementations often allocate extra capacity to reduce the frequency of reallocations.

images.description: Diagram showing a string object str2 with data and size members. Three states are shown: initial 'CS 102' (6 chars), reassigned to 'Computer Science' (16 chars), and concatenated to 'Computer Science is cool' (24 chars). Old arrays are crossed out with prohibition symbols to show deallocation.

title: String Comparison: C-Strings vs C++ Strings with Operators
summary: Comparison operators do not work with C-string char arrays (compare addresses). C++ strings perform correct lexicographic comparison with ==, <, > operators.
main_text: Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Quiz examples: "a" < "z" ? True. "a" > "aa" ? False (shorter string that matches prefix is less). "ab" < "ba" ? True (first char difference: 'a' < 'b'). "aab" < "aac" ? True (third char difference: 'b' < 'c'). Code example: char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if(str1 == "abc") does not work (compares pointer addresses). if(str2 == "abc") works, returns true. if(str1 < "aac") does not work. if(str2 < "aac") works, returns false (since "abc" > "aac"). string str3 = "acb"; if(str3 > str2) works, returns true.
notes_text: Lexicographic comparison works character by character from left to right. The first position where characters differ determines the result. If all characters match up to the length of the shorter string, the shorter string is considered less than the longer one. This is the same ordering as a dictionary. Understanding this is essential for sorting strings and for search algorithms.

images.description: Code example showing comparison operators failing with char arrays (comparing addresses) but working correctly with C++ strings, demonstrating lexicographic ordering results.

title: Summary: Objects, Dot Operator, Constructors, and Operators
summary: Key takeaways: iostream, fstream, and string are objects you already use. Initialize with = or constructors. Use dot operator for methods. Some operators are overloaded.
main_text: You have already used objects: iostream (cin and cout), now file streams and strings. There will be many more objects we can use from the C++ library. Can initialize at declaration by passing initial value in parentheses (known as a constructor). Use the dot operator to call an operation (function) on an object or access a data value. Some special operators can be used on certain object types (+, -, [], etc.) but you have to look them up. Example: #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, Using namespace std; int x; char line[80]; ifstream myfile(argv[1]); if(!myfile.fail()){ myfile >> x; } cin.getline(line, 80); cout << line << endl; cin, cout, ifstreams, and ofstreams are examples of objects.
notes_text: This summary ties everything together by pointing out that students have been using objects all along: cin and cout are objects of the iostream class, ifstream/ofstream are file stream objects. The dot operator is used to call member functions like myfile.fail() and cin.getline(). Understanding that these familiar tools are objects helps solidify the object-oriented concepts introduced in this unit.

images.description: Code example showing familiar objects in use: ifstream with constructor, myfile.fail() and cin.getline() using the dot operator, demonstrating that students have already been using objects.
